title: Supervised learning: regression & classification
summary: Learn a prediction function from labeled examples and test whether it generalizes.
html:
Learn a prediction function from labeled examples and test whether it generalizes.

Specify inputs, targets, and costs

Regression predicts a numerical target; classification predicts a discrete label or probability. The target must match the decision you want to make. Predicting whether a customer cancels is different from predicting whether an intervention would prevent cancellation.

Linear models are serious baselines

Linear regression combines features through weighted sums and commonly minimizes squared error. Logistic regression maps a linear score through a sigmoid for binary probabilities. Feature transformations permit nonlinear boundaries while retaining a linear model in the transformed space. Regularization constrains coefficient magnitude.

Bias, variance, and generalization

A model can underfit by missing structure or overfit by learning noise and sample-specific details. Training performance measures fit; held-out performance estimates generalization under the split assumptions. Learning curves compare performance as training data increases and can reveal whether more data is likely to help.

Thresholds implement decisions

A predicted probability is not yet an action. A threshold determines false positives and false negatives. Choose it using validation data and application costs. Report calibration as well as discrimination when probabilities inform decisions.

Worked example

Suppose missing a true defect costs 20 units and inspecting a non-defective item costs 1. Under a simplified binary decision model with calibrated probabilities, inspecting is worthwhile when expected missed-defect cost exceeds inspection cost. The optimal threshold depends on the exact cost matrix, not on the default value 0.5.

What goes wrong

A high random-split score does not prove future performance. Changes in acquisition, population, or policy can invalidate the learned relationship.

Check your understanding

Is logistic regression a regression or classification method in typical use?

Reveal the explanation

It models probabilities for classification despite its name. The logistic link transforms a real-valued linear score.

How the pieces connect

Define target → Prepare split → Fit baseline → Choose action. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it.

An operating model for supervised learning: regression & classification

Supervised learning generalizes from a sample to a stated future population. The label is not the decision: a probability must still be converted into an action under asymmetric costs, capacity limits, and human review. Better classification ranking does not automatically improve intervention outcomes.

The diagram is deliberately sequential, but real systems loop. A surprising result may expose a bad representation; a production incident may reveal a missing evaluation slice; a performance limit may require an algorithmic change. The point is to preserve the link between the abstract concept, the evidence you observe, and the decision you make next.

Worked system: a probability needs a policy

A fraud model gives a transaction a score of 0.62. That score is not an action. A review queue with capacity for one percent of transactions may require a high threshold; a low-friction extra verification step can be used more broadly; an irreversible decline may require a different threshold and a human appeal path. The same ranking model can support several policies, each with different costs for false positives and false negatives.

Start with an interpretable baseline and a held-out decision table. Inspect examples around the selected threshold, then compare the observed error mix with the people and resources the policy affects. A model that improves area under a curve can still make a workflow worse if it moves the wrong cases across the operating threshold.

Notebook: Measure the decision boundary, not only accuracy

Use this as an inspection pattern, not a drop-in production implementation. The specific values will change, but the habit remains: expose the assumption, calculate the boundary, and preserve the evidence that supports the next decision.

from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred).ravel()
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
recall = tp / (tp + fn)
print({"precision": precision, "recall": recall})
What to test next. 1. Define target: Specify label time, decision, and error costs. 2. Prepare split: Protect future, grouped, and held-out data. 3. Fit baseline: Use a simple interpretable model first. 4. Choose action: Calibrate and set a threshold for deployment.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Define target. Specify label time, decision, and error costs.
  2. Prepare split. Protect future, grouped, and held-out data.
  3. Fit baseline. Use a simple interpretable model first.
  4. Choose action. Calibrate and set a threshold for deployment.

Report a simple baseline, a held-out confusion matrix, calibration, and the operational threshold. Review examples around that threshold, because those are the cases the product will actually act on.

Questions that keep the chapter honest

AskWhy it mattersEvidence to collect
What assumptions does this method make?Every method encodes a view of data, hardware, or behavior.Inputs, representations, constraints, and cases outside the expected range.
What would make the result fail?Failure modes show where an aggregate result is fragile.Boundary cases, counterexamples, slices, and perturbations.
What decision changes if it improves?A metric only matters through an operational action.Baseline, threshold, cost, latency, and human-review consequences.
